title: How to Tell Your Story
excerpt: You do not need a dramatic conversion to have a story worth telling. You need to be honest about what was broken and what is different now.
body:
The man Jesus healed of blindness was dragged before the religious authorities and grilled about the theology of his healing. He did not have the answers. What he said instead became one of the most quoted lines in the Gospels: one thing I know, that though I was blind, now I see. He could not win the argument. He could only tell what happened to him. And that was enough.

Your story is the one piece of evidence no one can refute. They can argue with your doctrine. They cannot argue with your life. So it is worth learning to tell it well, which mostly means learning to tell it honestly.

## Drop the testimony performance

Many of us learned to tell our story in a polished, churchy register that no longer sounds like a human being. The dramatic before, the bright after, the bow on top. Real people can smell the polish, and the polish makes them trust you less. Tell it the way you would tell a friend what happened to you, because that is what it is. Plain words. Real details. The actual mess.

If your conversion was undramatic, do not invent drama. Some of us drifted toward God slowly, through a slow accumulation of small things, and that is a true and common story. The quiet stories are often more relatable than the spectacular ones, because most people's lives are quiet.

## Three honest parts

A story worth telling usually has three honest parts. What life was like before, told without exaggeration and without sanding off the parts that still embarrass you. What changed, the actual hinge, the moment or season when something shifted. And what is different now, told without pretending you arrived. Not before I was a wreck and now I am fixed, but before I was running and now I am being changed, still, slowly, with plenty left undone.

The self-implication matters. If your story makes you the hero who figured it out, no one is drawn in. If your story is honest about the ways you are still being undone, people lean closer, because that is where they live too.

## Name the real before

We are tempted to clean up the before so we look better. Resist it. The power of a testimony is in the honesty of the wreckage. I came to faith from atheism, and for years I told that story as if I had simply reasoned my way over. The truer version is that I was angry, certain, and afraid underneath the certainty, and grace found me before my arguments ran out. The truer version costs me something to tell. That cost is exactly why it lands.

## Keep it short and leave room

You do not need twenty minutes. Two or three are plenty, often less. A story told briefly invites a question. A story told exhaustively closes the conversation, because you have answered everything before they could ask anything. Tell the short version and stop. If they want more, they will ask, and the asking is where the real conversation begins.

## Connect it to their life, not yours

The point of telling your story is not to broadcast your biography. It is to put a door in the wall for someone else. So tell the part that connects to what they are carrying. If your friend is drowning in shame, tell the part about being forgiven. If they are exhausted by performing, tell the part about being loved before you earned anything. The same life has many doors. Open the one that faces them.

## You are a witness, not the verdict

A witness does not convict. A witness describes what he saw and steps down. You are not responsible for the outcome. You are responsible for the honesty. Tell what happened to you, plainly and humbly, and leave the rest to the One who actually changes people. The blind man did not convert the Pharisees. He just refused to deny what he could see now. That refusal, that simple loyalty to the truth of his own experience, was his whole testimony, and it was enough.

## This week

Write your story in three short paragraphs: the real before, the actual hinge, the honest now. Keep it under three hundred words. Read it out loud and listen for any sentence that sounds like a performance instead of a person, and cut it. Then keep that short, honest version where you can find it, so that when a friend opens a door with a question, you are not scrambling. You are ready to simply say what happened to you.
